claim: Back-propagating action potentials (bAPs) regulate synaptic plasticity by evoking voltage-dependent calcium influx throughout dendrites.
source: Back-propagating action potentials (bAPs) regulate synaptic plasticity by evoking voltage-dependent calcium influx throughout dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Attenuation of bAP amplitude in distal dendritic compartments alters plasticity in a location-specific manner by reducing bAP-dependent calcium influx.
source: Attenuation of bAP amplitude in distal dendritic compartments alters plasticity in a location-specific manner by reducing bAP-dependent calcium influx.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: bAPs fail to evoke calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) in a specific population of dendritic branches in mouse cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Here, we reveal that bAPs fail to evoke calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) in a specific population of dendritic branches in mouse cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal cells, despite evoking substantial VGCC-mediated calcium influx in sister branches.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including calcium imaging experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Low ΔCaAP branches contain VGCCs and successfully propagate bAPs in the absence of synaptic input.
source: These branches contain VGCCs and successfully propagate bAPs in the absence of synaptic input; nevertheless, they fail to exhibit bAP-evoked calcium influx due to a branch-specific reduction in bAP amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from glutamate puff experiments (Figure 3), loose-patch recordings (Figure 4), and voltage imaging (Figure 5).

claim: Low ΔCaAP branches fail to exhibit bAP-evoked calcium influx due to a branch-specific reduction in bAP amplitude.
source: These branches contain VGCCs and successfully propagate bAPs in the absence of synaptic input; nevertheless, they fail to exhibit bAP-evoked calcium influx due to a branch-specific reduction in bAP amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage imaging data showing reduced bAP amplitude in low ΔCaAP branches (Figure 5).

claim: Low ΔCaAP branches have more elaborate branch structure compared to sister branches, which causes a local reduction in electrotonic impedance and bAP amplitude.
source: We demonstrate that these branches have more elaborate branch structure compared to sister branches, which causes a local reduction in electrotonic impedance and bAP amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis (Figure 6) and computational modeling (Figure 7).

claim: bAPs still amplify synaptically-mediated calcium influx in low ΔCaAP branches because of differences in the voltage-dependence and kinetics of VGCCs and NMDA-type glutamate receptors.
source: Finally, we show that bAPs still amplify synaptically-mediated calcium influx in these branches because of differences in the voltage-dependence and kinetics of VGCCs and NMDA-type glutamate receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (Figures 1-2) and computational modeling of VGCC and NMDAR properties (Figure 8).

claim: Branch-specific compartmentalization of bAP-dependent calcium signals may provide a mechanism for neurons to diversify synaptic tuning across the dendritic tree.
source: Branch-specific compartmentalization of bAP-dependent calcium signals may provide a mechanism for neurons to diversify synaptic tuning across the dendritic tree.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: The outcome of plasticity induction protocols depends on the synaptic location within the dendritic tree.
source: However, other studies have shown that the outcome of plasticity induction protocols also depends on the synaptic location within the dendritic tree (Golding et al., 2002; Froemke et al., 2005; Sjöström and Häusser, 2006; Gordon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The same protocol can evoke a different sign, magnitude, or temporal profile of synaptic plasticity if applied to synapses in proximal or distal dendritic compartments.
source: The same protocol can evoke a different sign, magnitude, or temporal profile of synaptic plasticity if applied to synapses in proximal or distal dendritic compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: bAPs are attenuated as they propagate away from the soma.
source: Location-dependent plasticity rules vary along the proximodistal axis of dendrites because bAPs are attenuated as they propagate away from the soma (Regehr et al., 1989; Spruston et al., 1995; Golding et al., 2002; Waters et al., 2003; Froemke et al., 2005; Sjöström and Häusser, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In distal dendritic compartments, smaller amplitude bAPs evoke less voltage-dependent calcium-influx, such that induction protocols that usually evoke LTP result in LTD.
source: In distal dendritic compartments, smaller amplitude bAPs evoke less voltage-dependent calcium-influx, such that induction protocols that usually evoke LTP result in LTD (Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Sjöström and Häusser, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Experimentally boosting distal bAP amplitude can restore LTP by amplifying bAP-dependent calcium influx.
source: Experimentally boosting distal bAP amplitude can restore LTP by amplifying bAP-dependent calcium influx (Sjöström and Häusser, 2006), suggesting that location-dependent variation in synaptic plasticity rules is primarily determined by the local amplitude and timing of bAP-dependent calcium influx.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Location-dependent variation in synaptic plasticity rules is primarily determined by the local amplitude and timing of bAP-dependent calcium influx.
source: Experimentally boosting distal bAP amplitude can restore LTP by amplifying bAP-dependent calcium influx (Sjöström and Häusser, 2006), suggesting that location-dependent variation in synaptic plasticity rules is primarily determined by the local amplitude and timing of bAP-dependent calcium influx.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior work.

claim: Dendritic bAP-dependent calcium influx could be shaped by local variability in ion channel expression, synaptic inputs, or electrotonic impedance due to dendritic branch structure.
source: Dendritic bAP-dependent calcium influx could be shaped by local variability in ion channel expression, synaptic inputs, or electrotonic impedance due to dendritic branch structure (Rall and Rinzel, 1973; Vetter et al., 2001; Frick et al., 2004; Losonczy et al., 2008; Yaeger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Branch-specific variation in bAP-dependent calcium influx provides a potential mechanism for diversifying synaptic tuning across the dendritic tree.
source: Branch-specific variation in bAP-dependent calcium influx provides a potential mechanism for diversifying synaptic tuning across the dendritic tree, which is a core feature of computational models of neurons as hierarchical nonlinear integrators (Poirazi et al., 2003; Häusser and Mel, 2003; Francioni and Harnett, 2021; Bicknell and Häusser, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about functional implications, supported by citations to computational models.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) mediate bAP-evoked calcium influx and are responsible for various forms of plasticity.
source: These data suggest that voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which mediate bAP-evoked calcium influx and are responsible for various forms of plasticity (Kapur et al., 1998; Dolmetsch et al., 2001; Yasuda et al., 2003; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Scheuss et al., 2006, Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Brigidi et al., 2019), can be differentially activated by bAPs in a branch-specific manner within individual L2/3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VGCCs can be differentially activated by bAPs in a branch-specific manner within individual L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: These data suggest that voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which mediate bAP-evoked calcium influx and are responsible for various forms of plasticity (Kapur et al., 1998; Dolmetsch et al., 2001; Yasuda et al., 2003; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Scheuss et al., 2006, Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Brigidi et al., 2019), can be differentially activated by bAPs in a branch-specific manner within individual L2/3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: bAP-evoked calcium influx through VGCCs and bAP-dependent amplification of synaptically evoked calcium influx through NMDARs can be regulated independently in a branch-specific manner.
source: These data suggest that bAP-evoked calcium influx through VGCCs and bAP-dependent amplification of synaptically evoked calcium influx through NMDARs can be regulated independently in a branch-specific manner (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Holbro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations.

claim: The calcium signal evoked by glutamate puff was not an artifact of mechanical displacement due to the picospritzer.
source: The calcium signal was not an artifact of mechanical displacement due to the picospritzer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) and did not include an NMDAR component (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D), consistent with calcium influx mediated by VGCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The calcium signal evoked by glutamate puff did not include an NMDAR component.
source: The calcium signal was not an artifact of mechanical displacement due to the picospritzer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) and did not include an NMDAR component (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D), consistent with calcium influx mediated by VGCCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: All dendritic branches contain VGCCs, which can be opened by local depolarization.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that all dendritic branches contain VGCCs, which can be opened by local depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the glutamate puff and 4-AP experiments.

claim: bAP-dependent amplification of the remaining NMDAR-mediated calcium influx was observed in all dendritic spines examined in the presence of NBQX.
source: We observed bAP-dependent amplification of the remaining NMDAR-mediated calcium influx in all dendritic spines examined, despite fully blocking the depolarization evoked by glutamate uncaging (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: bAP-dependent voltage signals were observed in all branches, including those that did not exhibit bAP-evoked calcium influx.
source: Consistent with our results from Figure 4, we observed bAP-dependent voltage signals in all branches, including those that did not exhibit bAP-evoked calcium influx (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Branch complexity was inversely correlated with input resistance (R2 = 0.93 for λ = 145 µm).
source: Additionally, branch complexity was inversely correlated with input resistance (R2 = 0.93 for λ = 145 µm), confirming its validity as a measure of electrotonic properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Dendritic branch structure directly affects local dendritic excitability.
source: These data confirm that dendritic branch structure directly affects local dendritic excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulated cutting experiments.

claim: Dendritic branch structure affects the local amplitude of synaptic potentials, but has a minimal impact on the efficacy of synaptic input at depolarizing the soma.
source: Therefore, although dendritic branch structure affects the local amplitude of synaptic potentials, it has a minimal impact on the efficacy of synaptic input at depolarizing the soma.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational modeling data.

claim: VGCCs exhibit a dramatic drop-off of calcium influx for voltage steps peaking below –10 mV due to their steep voltage-sensitivity and long time constant.
source: Due to the steep voltage-sensitivity and long time constant of VGCCs (Figure 8A–B), they exhibit a dramatic drop-off of calcium influx for voltage steps peaking below –10 mV (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The interaction between open-probability and driving force minimizes differences in NMDAR-mediated calcium influx evoked across a wide range of voltages.
source: Although the open-probability of NMDARs is highly sensitive to peak voltage (Figure 8C–D), the interaction between open-probability and driving force minimizes differences in calcium influx evoked across a wide range of voltages (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 8.

claim: bAP-dependent calcium influx varies in a dendrite branch-specific manner in cortical L2/3 pyramidal cells due to branch-specific reductions in input resistance inherited from the local morphology of the dendritic tree.
source: Here, we show that bAP-dependent calcium influx varies in a dendrite branch-specific manner in cortical L2/3 pyramidal cells due to branch-specific reductions in input resistance inherited from the local morphology of the dendritic tree.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sections of the dendritic tree with more elaborate branch patterns have lower input resistance, leading to a branch-specific reduction in bAP amplitude.
source: Sections of the dendritic tree with more elaborate branch patterns have lower input resistance, leading to a branch-specific reduction in bAP amplitude.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by morphological analysis and computational modeling.

claim: Low ΔCaAP branches have a selective reduction in bAP-evoked calcium influx through VGCCs despite containing VGCCs and successfully propagating bAPs in the absence of synaptic input.
source: These branches have a selective reduction in bAP-evoked calcium influx through VGCCs despite containing VGCCs and successfully propagating bAPs in the absence of synaptic input.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 3-5.

claim: Low ΔCaAP branches maintain bAP-dependent amplification of synaptically-evoked calcium influx through NMDARs due to the shallower voltage-dependence and faster kinetics of the Mg2+-block of NMDARs.
source: However, these branches maintain bAP-dependent amplification of synaptically-evoked calcium influx through NMDARs due to the shallower voltage-dependence and faster kinetics of the Mg2+-block of NMDARs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 1-2 and modeling in Figure 8.

claim: Branch-specific variation in dendritic morphology shapes voltage-dependent calcium signals.
source: Branch-specific variation in dendritic morphology shapes voltage-dependent calcium signals
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Elaborate branching patterns reduce input resistance, local bAP amplitude, and bAP-evoked calcium influx because dendritic input resistance is proportional to the surface area of membrane.
source: Elaborate branching patterns reduce input resistance, local bAP amplitude, and bAP-evoked calcium influx because dendritic input resistance is proportional to the surface area of membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on established biophysical principles and the experimental data.

claim: The effect of branch structure on impedance is sufficient to cause the branch-specific differences observed.
source: Although our experiments show that the effect of branch structure on impedance is sufficient to cause the branch-specific differences we observed, additional mechanisms, such as variation in potassium channel density, may also contribute.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational modeling data.

claim: Additional mechanisms, such as variation in potassium channel density, may also contribute to branch-specific differences in bAP amplitude.
source: Although our experiments show that the effect of branch structure on impedance is sufficient to cause the branch-specific differences we observed, additional mechanisms, such as variation in potassium channel density, may also contribute.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative mechanisms.

claim: bAP-dependent activation of VGCCs is branch-specific in cortical L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Our data indicate that bAP-dependent activation of VGCCs is branch-specific in cortical L2/3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Each form of VGCC-mediated plasticity may be branch-specific in L2/3 pyramidal cells, at least with respect to their activation by bAPs.
source: First, because VGCC-mediated influx is responsible for multiple forms of synaptic and cellular plasticity (Kapur et al., 1998; Dolmetsch et al., 2001; Yasuda et al., 2003; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Scheuss et al., 2006, Brigidi et al., 2019), these data suggest that each of these forms of plasticity may be branch-specific in L2/3 pyramidal cells, at least with respect to their activation by bAPs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about plasticity implications.

claim: bAP-evoked calcium influx selectively drives LTD while bAP-dependent amplification of synaptic calcium influx selectively drives LTP.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that bAP-evoked calcium influx selectively drives LTD while bAP-dependent amplification of synaptic calcium influx selectively drives LTP (Feldman, 2000; Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ratio of LTD to LTP varies across branches in L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Therefore, identifying branches with a selective reduction in bAP-evoked calcium influx while maintaining bAP-dependent amplification of synaptically mediated calcium influx suggests that the ratio of LTD to LTP varies across branches in L2/3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and cited prior work on plasticity.

claim: The ratio of STDP-dependent depression to potentiation determines the cooperativity, strength, and sparsity of synaptic inputs.
source: Since the ratio of STDP-dependent depression to potentiation determines the cooperativity, strength, and sparsity of synaptic inputs (Song et al., 2000; Froemke et al., 2005; Sjöström and Häusser, 2006), our work suggests that synaptic tuning properties may vary in a branch-specific manner based on the local dendritic branch structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synaptic tuning properties may vary in a branch-specific manner based on the local dendritic branch structure.
source: Since the ratio of STDP-dependent depression to potentiation determines the cooperativity, strength, and sparsity of synaptic inputs (Song et al., 2000; Froemke et al., 2005; Sjöström and Häusser, 2006), our work suggests that synaptic tuning properties may vary in a branch-specific manner based on the local dendritic branch structure.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about functional implications.

claim: The experiments were conducted in juvenile mice (between P21 and P28).
source: Our experiments were conducted in juvenile mice (between P21 and P28).
evidence: This is a statement of experimental conditions.

claim: The dendritic branch structure is static after P21-P28 age.
source: Although the dendritic branch structure is static after this age (Koleske, 2013; Richards et al., 2020), it is possible that changes in channel composition dampen the effects of dendritic branch structure on excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Changes in channel composition may dampen the effects of dendritic branch structure on excitability.
source: Although the dendritic branch structure is static after this age (Koleske, 2013; Richards et al., 2020), it is possible that changes in channel composition dampen the effects of dendritic branch structure on excitability.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential developmental changes.

claim: Changes in dendritic excitability can occur as a result of synaptic plasticity induction.
source: We show that such effects are possible with compartment models (Figure 7F), and it is known that changes in dendritic excitability can occur as a result of synaptic plasticity induction (Frick et al., 2003; Frick et al., 2004; Losonczy et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Branch-specific variation in calcium-dependent plasticity signals may diversify synaptic tuning, which would increase dendritic computational capacity.
source: Second, branch-specific variation in calcium-dependent plasticity signals may diversify synaptic tuning, which would increase dendritic computational capacity (Poirazi et al., 2003; Häusser and Mel, 2003; Francioni and Harnett, 2021; Bicknell and Häusser, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about computational implications.

claim: Acute coronal slices were prepared from the somatosensory cortex of young adult, C57Bl/6 j wild-type mice between postnatal days P21-P28.
source: Acute coronal slices were prepared from the somatosensory cortex of young adult, C57Bl/6 j wild-type mice (Jackson Labs, Bar Harbor, ME) between postnatal days P21-P28.
evidence: This is a statement of experimental methods.

claim: The conduction velocity of bAPs in L2/3 dendrites is 154.9 µm/ms.
source: We found that the conduction velocity of bAPs in L2/3 dendrites is 154.9 µm/ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The somatic AP has a duration of about 0.94ms.
source: The somatic AP has a duration of about 0.94ms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: The spatial width of a propagating bAP is 145.6 µm.
source: To compute the spatial width of a propagating bAP, we multiplied the conduction velocity by the duration (154.9 µm/ms * 0.94ms = 145.6 µm).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental measurements.
